5. propose_test: an affordable experiment where the theories predict different results, with a decision rule that has a threshold.

justification.learned: Consumers are reachable: "Little Lotus products are available for sale on the company website, and swaddles have recently decreased in price from $98 to $85" (embrace-cnbc-price) — a $85 direct-to-consumer US swaddle, not a warmer. The warmer is clinical: "the Embrace® Nest was launched in 2011 in India, where it is widely used" (embrace-smg-launch), built for "settings where conventional incubators could be difficult to obtain" (embrace-ee-origin). Warmth worry is anecdote (embrace-yahoo-origin); the SIDS link is only a company claim (embrace-her-sids). Investors need commercial scale (embrace-gsb-investors). No source shows consumer demand, price response or margin: demand unknown.
justification.uncertain: Whether parents commit real money, and whether the cause is medical necessity (T1) or night-check relief (T2): nothing measures willingness to pay for a home warmer, only the $85 swaddle anchor (embrace-cnbc-price). Unknown whether a SIDS/medical framing for a home device is legally usable in 2016 — a magazine claim (embrace-her-sids) is not clearance, so T1's mechanism could be blocked. Scale and margin unknown. Deposits, visitor counts and €20,000 are proposed parameters, not market facts.
justification.why_next: A deposit test separates T1 from T2: each names a different cause, predicting different winners and buyer mix (embrace-cnbc-price, embrace-yahoo-origin, embrace-her-sids, embrace-ee-origin). T1: buyers are parents of pre-term/low-birth-weight babies seeking medical risk reduction, so the clinician-endorsed thermal-safety kit out-converts and depositors concentrate among LBW parents. T2: buyers are any exhausted new parents buying night-check relief, so the monitor bundle wins and depositors resemble general new parents. Arms share price, layout, channel and creative; random assignment and depositor mix address creative, targeting and novelty alternatives. Fits €20,000 and 12 weeks.

justification.learned: Capability and channel are shown; demand is not. Cotral Lab is "the world's No.1 manufacturer of custom-molded hearing protection" whose products "will continue to be distributed primarily through direct channels to end-user companies" (ctl-channel); impressions are "taken directly on-site" for employees (ctl-onsite), and IT1 addresses employees (ctl-it1) — an employer-paid B2B route with no evidence of a consumer paying. Sleep demand is unknown (T2).
justification.uncertain: No source shows individual willingness to pay, a French consumer price for custom moulds, repeat use or unit economics; Cotral's financials are not public. T2's "medical-grade" framing raises a regulatory question I have no source for. Whether Cotral would join a pilot, or a partner would take impressions, is unverified — the company has not been contacted. One competitor result (etymotic-er20xs) went unread. The 6-of-60 threshold is a coarse proposed screen.
justification.why_next: The deposit pilot separates T1 from T2 because both arms get identical product, €180 price, €30 deposit and fulfilment, differing only in segment and positioning: T1 predicts musicians commit at a premium, T2 predicts noise-sensitive sleepers do. Real money and a live fitting test payer willingness, not stated intent; the B2B-only route in ctl-channel and ctl-onsite is why the offer runs through a borrowed fitting partner, and ctl-filter makes the attribute real. It stays a partner trial, not a product line, because no source shows consumer demand to size against (bockstael-2015-looks and minuendo-claim leave the sound-quality mechanism contested).

You are a strategy analyst investigating an opportunity for a manufacturer. Use these tools:
read_brief {} : read the company, the question and your budgets.
frame_problem {"objective":"...","constraints":["..."],"alternatives":["..."]} : state the real objective and the options, including ones the question did not suggest. Accepted once.
search_evidence {"query":"..."} : keyword search of the evidence. Uses one search.
challenge_theory {"theory_id":"T1","query":"..."} : search for evidence that could prove a theory wrong. Uses one search.
read_source {"id":"..."} : read a result found by search.
add_theory {"claim":"...","who_benefits":"...","why_behaviour_changes":"...","how_value_is_captured":"...","assumptions":["..."],"predictions":["..."]} : add one causal theory of value. Returns its id.
assess_evidence {"theory_id":"T1","evidence_id":"...","direction":"supports or contradicts or neutral","quote":"exact words from the source","evidence_kind":"company_assertion or customer_observation or independent_study or regulation or analogy or market_fact","does_not_show":"what this evidence cannot establish"} : say how evidence bears on a theory, honestly. Use neutral if it does neither.
propose_test {"name":"...","theories":["T1","T2"],"method":"...","sample":"...","measure":"...","prediction_by_theory":{"T1":"...","T2":"..."},"decision_rule":"...","cost_eur":N,"weeks":N} : design an experiment where the theories predict different results.
revise_theory {"theory_id":"T1","status":"kept or revised or rejected","reason":"...","new_claim":"the changed claim, or none","evidence_ids":["..."]} : update a theory after new evidence.
finish {"recommendation":"...","target_customer":"...","value_proposition":"...","favoured_theory":"T1","next_action":"...","uncertainty":"...","would_change_if":["..."],"evidence_ids":["..."]} : end the investigation.

Reply with one JSON object: {"name": "<tool>", "arguments": {...}}. A user turn that starts with "Tool result:" is the output of your call. End by calling finish.

Work like a scientist, not a consultant.
1. read_brief, then frame_problem. List at least three alternatives, including no expansion and options the question did not suggest.
2. Search before you theorise. Find out what the company already sells to individual buyers, and do not assume. Read at least three sources.
3. add_theory at least twice, and a third time if you have a different cause. A theory is a causal explanation of why people behave as they do, not advice. Do not write "the company should". Each theory needs a different cause: who benefits, why they would change behaviour, how the manufacturer captures value. Give assumptions, and predictions someone could measure.
For example, from eyewear: "People treat glasses as a medical necessity. If they came to see them as fashion, they would own several pairs, so a maker that controls design and retail could earn premium prices." A rival theory would name a different cause.
4. assess_evidence for every theory, quoting the source's exact words. Say what kind of evidence it is and what it cannot show. A company's own claim is not proof of demand. Use challenge_theory to look for evidence that could prove your favoured theory wrong. If you find nothing against it, say so. Never force a contradiction.
5. propose_test: an affordable experiment where the theories predict different results, with a decision rule that has a threshold.
6. If new evidence arrives, read it and use revise_theory.
7. finish. Say what you recommend, the next action, what is uncertain, and what would change your mind.

Every number or fact you present as observed must come from a source you read. Numbers you propose, such as a test's sample, budget, duration, threshold or an estimate, are allowed when you label them as proposed or estimated. Your theories are hypotheses, not facts. Results marked SIMULATED are not real demand, so never cite one in finish.

A controller opens the tools for each stage, and each tool result lists them. Before you finish you will also use:
decline_test {"reason":"..."} : say why more information is not worth its cost here, instead of proposing a test.
state_position {"favoured_theory":"T1","recommendation":"...","beliefs":{"T1":"likely","T2":"uncertain"}} : say what you believe now, rating each theory very unlikely, unlikely, uncertain, likely or very likely. finish then also takes "beliefs".
A SIMULATED result is a what-if exercise. Reason as if it were real, and say what it would mean for your theories. A result can change nothing. Still keep it out of the evidence you cite.

Each turn shows the current state of the investigation, including what you already tried. Do not repeat a call listed there.

Beneficials already ship to amateurs: beetles go to farmers and home gardeners in spring (koppert-wsu-shipped). France bans amateur phytosanitary sales from January 2019 (koppert-agro-ban, 2017): positioning, not demand. The one consumer observation (koppert-martha-visit) shows paying for expert service, not status — I first misread it as support for T2. No evidence of gardener demand, price points or repeat rates. T1 uncertain; T2 unlikely, no source bears on it.
justification.uncertain: Unmeasured: demand itself — no source I read gives gardener purchase rates, price points or repeat use, so whether a consumer line sells in the Netherlands or France is unknown. Nor the mechanism: koppert-lo-canada and koppert-wsu-shipped show amateur products exist and ship, koppert-martha-visit one rich buyer of a bespoke service; none shows why ordinary gardeners pay, so T1 and T2 stay unseparated. Margins and an EU-ready consumer format are unknown. A price test fits 20000 EUR.
justification.why_next: The open question is why a home gardener would pay a premium. T1 (functional value, from koppert-lo-canada and koppert-wsu-shipped) predicts price sensitivity, since the benefit is practical and comparable to cheaper alternatives; T2 (status or eco-signalling, resting only on koppert-martha-visit) predicts weak sensitivity or a premium effect. Varying only price on an identical pre-order separates them; a paid deposit measures commitment, not intent. Alternatives tracked: bargain-hunting in the low cell, audience mix (randomised same ad set), and the small deposit overstating purchase, so rates are a ceiling.

You are a strategy analyst investigating an opportunity for a manufacturer. Use these tools:
read_brief {} : read the company, the question and your budgets.
frame_problem {"objective":"...","constraints":["..."],"alternatives":["..."]} : state the real objective and the options, including ones the question did not suggest. Accepted once.
search_evidence {"query":"..."} : keyword search of the evidence. Uses one search.
challenge_theory {"theory_id":"T1","query":"..."} : search for evidence that could prove a theory wrong. Uses one search.
read_source {"id":"..."} : read a result found by search.
add_theory {"claim":"...","who_benefits":"...","why_behaviour_changes":"...","how_value_is_captured":"...","assumptions":["..."],"predictions":["..."]} : add one causal theory of value. Returns its id.
assess_evidence {"theory_id":"T1","evidence_id":"...","direction":"supports or contradicts or neutral","quote":"exact words from the source","evidence_kind":"company_assertion or customer_observation or independent_study or regulation or analogy or market_fact","does_not_show":"what this evidence cannot establish"} : say how evidence bears on a theory, honestly. Use neutral if it does neither.
propose_test {"name":"...","theories":["T1","T2"],"method":"...","sample":"...","measure":"...","prediction_by_theory":{"T1":"...","T2":"..."},"decision_rule":"...","cost_eur":N,"weeks":N} : design an experiment where the theories predict different results.
revise_theory {"theory_id":"T1","status":"kept or revised or rejected","reason":"...","new_claim":"the changed claim, or none","evidence_ids":["..."]} : update a theory after new evidence.
finish {"recommendation":"...","target_customer":"...","value_proposition":"...","favoured_theory":"T1","next_action":"...","uncertainty":"...","would_change_if":["..."],"evidence_ids":["..."]} : end the investigation.

Reply with one JSON object: {"name": "<tool>", "arguments": {...}}. A user turn that starts with "Tool result:" is the output of your call. End by calling finish.

Work like a scientist, not a consultant.
1. read_brief, then frame_problem. List at least three alternatives, including no expansion and options the question did not suggest.
2. Search before you theorise. Find out what the company already sells to individual buyers, and do not assume. Read at least three sources.
3. add_theory at least twice, and a third time if you have a different cause. A theory is a causal explanation of why people behave as they do, not advice. Do not write "the company should". Each theory needs a different cause: who benefits, why they would change behaviour, how the manufacturer captures value. Give assumptions, and predictions someone could measure.
For example, from eyewear: "People treat glasses as a medical necessity. If they came to see them as fashion, they would own several pairs, so a maker that controls design and retail could earn premium prices." A rival theory would name a different cause.
4. assess_evidence for every theory, quoting the source's exact words. Say what kind of evidence it is and what it cannot show. A company's own claim is not proof of demand. Use challenge_theory to look for evidence that could prove your favoured theory wrong. If you find nothing against it, say so. Never force a contradiction.
5. propose_test: an affordable experiment where the theories predict different results, with a decision rule that has a threshold.
6. If new evidence arrives, read it and use revise_theory.
7. finish. Say what you recommend, the next action, what is uncertain, and what would change your mind.

Every number or fact you present as observed must come from a source you read. Numbers you propose, such as a test's sample, budget, duration, threshold or an estimate, are allowed when you label them as proposed or estimated. Your theories are hypotheses, not facts. Results marked SIMULATED are not real demand, so never cite one in finish.

A controller opens the tools for each stage, and each tool result lists them. Before you finish you will also use:
decline_test {"reason":"..."} : say why more information is not worth its cost here, instead of proposing a test.
state_position {"favoured_theory":"T1","recommendation":"...","beliefs":{"T1":"likely","T2":"uncertain"}} : say what you believe now, rating each theory very unlikely, unlikely, uncertain, likely or very likely. finish then also takes "beliefs".
A SIMULATED result is a what-if exercise. Reason as if it were real, and say what it would mean for your theories. A result can change nothing. Still keep it out of the evidence you cite.

Each turn shows the current state of the investigation, including what you already tried. Do not repeat a call listed there.

justification.learned: Andis already sells to individuals, so the question is further differentiation, not entry. andis-1997-home-kits: products were "useful to consumers as well as to professional barbers", so it "began to develop personal grooming products... to use at home". andis-home-line shows a live home line; andis-athome-prices lists kits at $59.99 and $24.99, so differentiation means going above ~$60. Home demand is observed: andis-wahl-6-million reports the category "up 42%"; andis-wahl-10-percent expects "about 10% more of the USA will switch" to home cutting. No source shows premium willingness to pay; andis-attest-20-dollars quotes a buyer treating "$20 from Amazon" as decisive.
justification.uncertain: Premium take-up above Andis's $59.99 home top is unmeasured; growth (andis-wahl-6-million, andis-wahl-10-percent) says nothing about paying more, and both are trade reportage, not Andis data. T1 and T2 differ only in cause, both predicting premium buying, so nothing read separates them; a price-anchor reading (andis-attest-20-dollars: a buyer comparing clippers to "$20") predicts near-zero take-up. Also unmeasured: Andis's premium-kit margins and the professional channel's performance.
justification.why_next: T1 and T2 are not separated by anything read: andis-home-line is a company claim fitting either, and category growth (andis-wahl-6-million, andis-wahl-10-percent) speaks to participation, not to why anyone pays more. A paid-offer test separates them because each mechanism predicts a different pattern of deposits under identical presentation: T1 predicts the professional-precision arm wins, T2 the convenience arm, and the price-anchor reading in andis-attest-20-dollars predicts both premium arms fail against the $59 kit - the outcome that would send Andis toward the professional/groomer option. Stated preference would not separate them; only a deposit does.
